title: Chapter 5 Drill: Peripheral Nerve and Motor Neuron Disease

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes, obesity, and hypertension has typical chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy confirmed by electrodiagnostic criteria. Which first-line therapy is preferred in this patient?
options: High-dose oral prednisone for many months
items.explanation: Immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange are all first-line options for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. In patients with diabetes, hypertension, or obesity, immunoglobulin avoids the metabolic and cardiovascular risks of prolonged steroid therapy. Azathioprine and cyclophosphamide are reserved as second-line agents because evidence for them is weaker and toxicity is greater. Therapy is often continued at lower doses at set intervals to prevent relapse, with periodic attempts to taper.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman takes a high-dose over-the-counter supplement for hair loss. She develops progressive numbness of the hands and feet with sensory ataxia, absent reflexes, and preserved strength. Which vitamin is most likely responsible?
items.explanation: Chronic intake of pyridoxine in large amounts, generally above 100 mg per day, damages the dorsal root ganglia and causes a sensory neuronopathy with sensory ataxia. Deficiency of B6 can also cause neuropathy, but this patient takes a surplus. Excess thiamine, cobalamin, and riboflavin are not recognized causes of neuropathy and are generally non-toxic. Reversal usually requires stopping the supplement, and recovery is often incomplete in severe cases.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man has weakness and atrophy of one hand and forearm that worsens with neck flexion, and cervical MRI in flexion shows anterior displacement of the posterior dural sac. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Monomelic amyotrophy of the hand and forearm (Hirayama disease)
items.explanation: Hirayama disease affects young men with unilateral hand and forearm atrophy that stops progressing after a few years, and flexion MRI shows forward shift of the dura compressing the lower cervical cord. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progresses relentlessly. Syringomyelia produces dissociated sensory loss, and multifocal motor neuropathy shows conduction block. Cervical collar immobilization to limit neck flexion typically stabilizes the disorder and prevents progression.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has bilateral facial weakness that evolved over 3 days, with facial nerve involvement on both sides, parotid swelling, uveitis, and low-grade fever. Chest imaging shows hilar adenopathy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Idiopathic Bell palsy on both sides
Neurosarcoidosis presenting as uveoparotid fever (Heerfordt syndrome)
items.explanation: The combination of facial nerve palsy, parotid enlargement, anterior uveitis, and fever is Heerfordt syndrome, a form of neurosarcoidosis, and hilar adenopathy supports it. Simultaneous bilateral facial palsy should prompt a search for sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, and Guillain-Barre syndrome, rather than a diagnosis of idiopathic palsy. Ramsay Hunt is unilateral with vesicles, and myasthenia is fatigable.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man treated for heart rhythm disturbance with a long-term antiarrhythmic develops tremor, a slowly progressive demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and corneal microdeposits. Which drug is the most likely cause?
items.explanation: Amiodarone can cause a sensorimotor polyneuropathy with demyelinating features, tremor, optic neuropathy, and corneal microdeposits, along with thyroid, pulmonary, and hepatic toxicity. The neuropathy improves slowly after withdrawal. Metoprolol, digoxin, and verapamil are not associated with a demyelinating neuropathy or corneal deposits. Thyroid, liver, and pulmonary function should be monitored in any patient who remains on this drug.

items.stem: A technician performs an ulnar nerve conduction study on a very cold hand with a skin temperature of 27 degrees Celsius. What effect on the results should be expected if the hand is not warmed?
options: Falsely slowed velocity with prolonged latencies and larger amplitudes
Falsely fast velocity with shortened latencies and slightly smaller amplitudes
No change in velocity but a lower amplitude due to conduction block
Absent F waves with normal distal latency
items.explanation: Cooling slows the kinetics of sodium channel inactivation, so conduction velocity falls and latencies lengthen, while the longer duration of the potential can raise amplitude. A cold limb can therefore mimic mild demyelination or carpal tunnel syndrome. Warming to at least 32 degrees Celsius at the hand is standard before interpreting a study. This is why limb temperature is always checked and the limb warmed before any study is called abnormal.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has sudden periorbital pain followed by right ptosis and an eye that is down and out. The pupil is normal in size and reactive. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Compression of the nerve by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Ischemic infarction of the central fibers of the oculomotor nerve
items.explanation: Pupil-sparing third nerve palsy with pain in a patient with vascular risk factors usually results from microvascular infarction of the nerve core, because pupillary fibers lie peripherally and receive collateral supply. Aneurysmal compression typically involves the pupil early. Nuclear demyelination and cavernous thrombosis would produce additional signs, and recovery of the diabetic form occurs over about three months.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has numbness and burning of the right thumb, index, and middle fingers and a 6 week history of neck pain. Median and ulnar sensory responses are normal, but median motor amplitude is reduced and needle examination shows fibrillations in C6 and C7 muscles including the paraspinals. What does the normal sensory response despite numbness indicate?
options: A lesion of the distal median nerve at the wrist
A lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
A pure small fiber sensory neuropathy
A lesion of the posterior cord
items.explanation: In radiculopathy the dorsal root ganglion lies outside the foramen, so the peripheral sensory axon stays connected to its cell body and the sensory response remains normal even with a dense sensory deficit. Paraspinal fibrillations localize the lesion to the root or ventral ramus. A distal median lesion or plexus lesion would lower the sensory amplitude.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man develops painless wrist drop after leaning on his elbow during a long exam, and 6 months earlier had a painless foot drop that resolved. Nerve conduction studies show diffuse prolonged distal latencies and focal slowing at common compression sites. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: Deletion of one copy of PMP22
Point mutation in GJB1 on the X chromosome
items.explanation: Recurrent painless pressure palsies with focal slowing at entrapment sites define hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies, caused by a deletion of one PMP22 copy. Duplication of the same gene causes the diffuse demyelinating CMT1A. GJB1 mutations cause X-linked CMT, and transthyretin mutations cause a painful amyloid neuropathy. Genetic testing for the deletion confirms the diagnosis and avoids unnecessary nerve biopsy.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man with long-standing diabetes has lightheadedness on standing, constipation, impotence, and a fixed heart rate. Systolic pressure drops by 40 mm Hg on standing without a rise in heart rate. What is the best initial nonpharmacologic strategy for orthostatic hypotension in this autonomic neuropathy?
options: Strict fluid restriction to 1 liter daily
Lying flat with the head down at night
Increased fluid and salt intake, compression garments, and slow postural changes
items.explanation: Management of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension begins with volume expansion through fluid and sodium, abdominal binders or stockings, slow position changes, and head-up sleeping to limit nocturnal natriuresis. Drugs such as fludrocortisone, midodrine, or droxidopa are added if needed. Fluid restriction, head-down sleeping, and anticholinergics worsen the problem. Medications such as fludrocortisone, midodrine, or droxidopa are added only when these measures fail.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has severe right ear pain followed by a right facial palsy, vesicles in the external auditory canal, and vertigo with hearing loss. Which pathogen causes this syndrome, and which treatment is added to corticosteroids?
options: Herpes simplex virus type 1, with no antiviral
Varicella zoster virus, with an antiviral such as valacyclovir
items.explanation: Reactivation of varicella zoster in the geniculate ganglion causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome, with ear vesicles, facial palsy, and often hearing loss and vertigo from eighth nerve involvement. It carries a poorer prognosis than idiopathic Bell palsy, and treatment combines prednisone with an antiviral. Lyme disease and Epstein-Barr virus are not responsible. Early treatment within three days improves the chance of recovering facial function and reduces lasting deafness.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has had slowly progressive proximal leg weakness since childhood, with difficulty climbing stairs, tongue-sparing fasciculations in the hands, and areflexia. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated and an SMN1 deletion is found with four copies of SMN2. Which spinal muscular atrophy type is most likely?
options: Type 0, a severe prenatal onset form
Type 1, with inability to sit unsupported
Type 3, with onset after the ability to walk was acquired
Type 4, with onset only after age 30
items.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy type 3 begins after independent walking is achieved and progresses slowly, with proximal weakness, and higher SMN2 copy numbers correlate with milder disease. Type 0 occurs in utero, and type 1 presents before 6 months and does not allow sitting. Type 4 begins in adulthood and has a still milder course. Walking ability may be lost later in life, but life expectancy is usually normal in this type.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a slowly progressive distal axonal neuropathy with prominent foot drop and early onset of spastic features. Median motor conduction velocity is 52 m/s. Her father and two siblings are affected. What does the preserved velocity indicate?
options: A demyelinating form of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, type 1
An axonal form of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, type 2
items.explanation: In hereditary neuropathy a median motor velocity above about 38 m/s with reduced amplitudes indicates the axonal type 2 form, and type 1 shows uniform velocities below 38 m/s. Mutations in MFN2 are the most common cause of type 2 disease. Pressure palsy syndromes show focal, not uniform, slowing, and acquired chronic demyelination shows nonuniform slowing.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has weight loss of 10 kilograms, then severe pain in the right anterior thigh followed by quadriceps weakness and atrophy. Which treatment aspect is best supported for diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy?
options: Pain control and supportive care, with consideration of immunotherapy in severe cases
Immediate surgical decompression of the lumbar roots and lumbosacral plexus exploration
items.explanation: Diabetic amyotrophy is a microvasculitic radiculoplexus neuropathy that typically improves over months to years. Management is analgesia, physical therapy, and glycemic optimization, and immunotherapy such as glucocorticoids may be considered in progressive disease, although evidence is limited. Decompression, radiation, and anticoagulation have no role in this self-limited process. Recovery is slow, often taking a year or more, and pain tends to resolve earlier than strength.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has two years of symmetric numbness of the toes spreading to the ankles, with reduced vibration sense and absent ankle jerks. Strength is normal. She takes no medications and has no family history. Which laboratory panel is the most useful first-line evaluation for this length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy?
options: Antinuclear antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, rheumatoid factor, complement levels, and cryoglobulins
Fasting glucose or glucose tolerance, vitamin B12, and serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation
Anti-ganglioside antibodies and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
Genetic panel for hereditary neuropathies and nerve biopsy
items.explanation: Diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance, B12 deficiency, and monoclonal gammopathy are the most common identifiable and treatable causes of an axonal length-dependent polyneuropathy, so they form the core initial screen. Vasculitis serology, ganglioside antibodies, spinal fluid, genetic panels, and biopsy are reserved for atypical, rapid, asymmetric, or demyelinating presentations. Results of this screen guide whether more extensive testing is justified in the following weeks.

items.stem: A 2-month-old infant has marked hypotonia, a bell-shaped chest, a weak cry, and tongue fasciculations. Genetic testing shows homozygous deletion of exon 7 of SMN1 and two copies of SMN2. Which therapy class changes the course of disease?
options: SMN-targeted therapies such as nusinersen, risdiplam, or onasemnogene gene therapy
items.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy results from loss of SMN1, and therapies that increase SMN protein transform the natural history: the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen, the splicing modifier risdiplam, and gene replacement with onasemnogene abeparvovec. Early treatment, ideally before symptoms, gives the best results. Steroids, pyridostigmine, and immunoglobulin do not alter the SMN pathway. Treatment should start as early as possible, since lost motor neurons cannot be restored later.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman with ovarian cancer receives cisplatin and develops numbness of the hands and feet, loss of proprioception, and sensory ataxia with preserved strength. Which mechanism underlies this chemotherapy neuropathy?
options: Disruption of microtubule transport in motor axons only
Damage to dorsal root ganglion neurons
items.explanation: Platinum agents accumulate in the dorsal root ganglia and cause a dose-dependent sensory neuronopathy, with ataxia that may progress after the drug is stopped, a phenomenon called coasting. Vinca alkaloids and taxanes affect microtubules and cause an axonal sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy. Complement mediated demyelination and junction blockade are not features of platinum toxicity. Symptoms can worsen for weeks after the final dose before stabilizing, which affects counseling about prognosis.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has sudden bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and absent ankle reflexes after heavy lifting. Which lesion is most likely?
options: Cauda equina compression from a large central lumbar disc herniation
Conus medullaris infarction from aortic dissection
items.explanation: Saddle anesthesia, retention, bilateral leg weakness, and areflexia indicate involvement of the lumbosacral roots in the cauda equina, which constitutes a surgical emergency in the setting of a massive central disc herniation. Conus lesions often cause hyperreflexia and early sphincter loss. Bilateral peroneal palsies spare sphincter function, and Guillain-Barre syndrome rarely presents so abruptly after lifting.

items.stem: A 45-year-old hiker from the northeastern United States has a left facial palsy, followed by a painful asymmetric radiculoneuropathy in the trunk. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. Which treatment is indicated?
items.explanation: Lyme neuroborreliosis commonly causes cranial neuropathies, especially facial palsy, with painful radiculoneuritis and lymphocytic meningitis. Parenteral ceftriaxone is standard for neurologic involvement beyond isolated facial palsy, while oral doxycycline may suffice for isolated seventh nerve palsy. Steroids alone, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin do not eradicate the spirochete. Duration is usually two to three weeks, and the cerebrospinal fluid is rechecked if symptoms persist.

items.stem: A 50-year-old overweight man has burning and numbness over the anterolateral right thigh that worsens with standing and wearing a tight belt. Strength and reflexes are normal. Which nerve is affected?
options: Femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
items.explanation: Meralgia paresthetica is entrapment of the purely sensory lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the inguinal ligament, causing burning and numbness of the anterolateral thigh without weakness or reflex change. Femoral neuropathy weakens knee extension and reduces the knee jerk. Obturator lesions affect the medial thigh and adduction, and ilioinguinal lesions affect the groin. Weight loss, avoiding tight clothing, and local injection of corticosteroid often relieve symptoms without surgery.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has progressive difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Needle examination of the quadriceps shows small, short, polyphasic motor units with early recruitment and normal firing rates. Which process is most consistent with these findings?
options: A chronic neurogenic process with reinnervation
Anterior horn cell loss with giant units
A myopathic process with loss of fibers per motor unit
items.explanation: Myopathy drops the number of working fibers within each motor unit, producing small, brief, polyphasic potentials, and the muscle needs many units early to generate force. Neurogenic disease gives large, long units with reduced recruitment and a rapid firing rate. Poor effort produces a normal unit morphology with limited recruitment. Poor effort, by contrast, shows normal unit shapes with limited recruitment, which is why morphology guides the interpretation.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1c of 13 percent lowers it to 7 percent over three months. Two months later he develops severe burning pain in the feet and orthostatic lightheadedness. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy unmasked by insulin
Treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes after rapid glycemic correction
Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy from microvasculitis of nerves
items.explanation: A rapid fall in glycemia, particularly an A1c drop of more than 2 points over three months, can precipitate painful small fiber and autonomic neuropathy, termed treatment-induced neuropathy. Management is slow glycemic adjustment and symptomatic pain therapy. Radiculoplexus neuropathy is an asymmetric proximal syndrome, and B6 toxicity would produce a large fiber sensory neuronopathy without autonomic failure.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy, skin hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, leg edema, and papilledema. Imaging shows sclerotic bone lesions. Which serum marker is most useful in supporting the diagnosis?
options: Elevated anti-GM1 antibody titer on serum testing
items.explanation: POEMS syndrome features polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, a monoclonal plasma cell disorder usually of lambda type, and skin changes, with sclerotic bone lesions and markedly raised vascular endothelial growth factor. Treatment targets the plasma cell clone with radiation of a solitary lesion or systemic therapy. Anti-GM1, copper, and creatine kinase are unrelated. Treating the underlying plasma cell process improves the neuropathy, which otherwise progresses over many months.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has weakness of the right hand with thumb and finger flexion lost and atrophy of the forearm, but reports no sensory loss. A lesion in which location can be distinguished by needle examination of the pronator teres?
options: Suprascapular nerve versus upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Anterior interosseous nerve versus proximal median nerve
items.explanation: The anterior interosseous branch leaves the median nerve below the elbow and spares the pronator teres, which is innervated higher. Abnormal pronator teres activity therefore places the lesion at or above the branch point, in the proximal median nerve, while a normal pronator teres supports a branch lesion. The other pairs do not rely on pronator teres.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man living near an old industrial site has four weeks of abdominal pain, then progressive weakness and burning pain in the feet. Skin shows Mees lines on the nails and hyperkeratosis. Which toxin is most likely responsible?
items.explanation: Arsenic produces a painful sensorimotor axonal neuropathy that can mimic Guillain-Barre syndrome, with gastrointestinal symptoms, hyperkeratosis, and transverse white nail bands called Mees lines. Diagnosis rests on a 24 hour urine arsenic level. Lead tends to produce a predominantly motor radial neuropathy, and thallium typically causes alopecia and painful neuropathy within days. Chelation therapy is considered once the exposure is confirmed and the source is removed from the environment.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has slowly progressive stiffness and weakness of both legs since adolescence. Her father has a similar gait disorder. Sensation is normal, and brain and spine imaging are unremarkable. Mutation in which gene is the most common cause of this autosomal dominant syndrome?
options: SMN1, encoding survival motor neuron protein
items.explanation: Pure hereditary spastic paraplegia with an autosomal dominant pedigree is most often caused by mutations in SPAST, which encodes spastin and accounts for roughly 40 percent of dominant cases. SMN1 deficiency causes spinal muscular atrophy, PMP22 changes cause peripheral neuropathies, and frataxin deficiency causes Friedreich ataxia. Genetic testing helps family counseling, and treatment is symptomatic with stretching, baclofen, and rehabilitation.

items.stem: A 44-year-old runner has burning pain and numbness of the sole of the right foot that is worse at night and after exercise. Tinel sign is positive behind the medial malleolus. Which structure is compressed?
options: Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head and neck
Tibial nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum
Sural nerve at the lateral malleolus
Deep peroneal nerve at the ankle
items.explanation: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the posterior tibial nerve or its plantar branches under the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus, producing plantar paresthesias that worsen with activity. The common peroneal nerve supplies the dorsum and lateral leg. The sural nerve supplies the lateral foot, and the deep peroneal supplies the first web space.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman develops a foot drop after losing weight rapidly and crossing her legs habitually. She has weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, but normal inversion and a normal ankle jerk. Which finding best supports a peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head over L5 radiculopathy?
options: Normal needle examination of the tibialis posterior
Weak hip abduction with reduced gluteus medius power
items.explanation: The tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve through the L5 root, so it stays normal when the lesion lies in the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head, and abnormal in L5 radiculopathy. Weak hip abduction and L5 paraspinal fibrillations support a root lesion. Sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot occurs in both.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has asymmetric weakness of the right hand and forearm with cramps and fasciculations but no sensory loss and normal reflexes. Motor conduction block is seen in the right median and ulnar nerves. Which treatment should be avoided?
items.explanation: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block responds to immunoglobulin, and glucocorticoids and plasma exchange are generally ineffective and may cause worsening. Subcutaneous immunoglobulin is an option for maintenance, and cyclophosphamide is reserved for refractory cases. Anti-GM1 antibodies are present in some patients, but the diagnosis rests on electrodiagnostic features. Because relapses are common after therapy, long-term follow-up with repeated examination is needed.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man develops a complete right peroneal nerve palsy after a knee dislocation. Needle examination of the tibialis anterior is performed on day 4 and shows no spontaneous activity and absent voluntary units. When are fibrillation potentials most reliably expected in distal limb muscles after axonal transection?
options: Within the first 24 hours in every muscle
About 3 to 4 weeks after the injury in distal muscles
Only after reinnervation begins several months later in all muscles
Never, because they signal only muscle disease
items.explanation: Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves need time to appear after denervation, roughly 10 to 14 days in proximal muscles and up to 3 to 4 weeks in distal ones. A study on day 4 therefore cannot grade the lesion, although absent recruitment is already informative. These potentials occur in both neuropathic and some myopathic disorders and are not confined to muscle disease.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has a two month course of fever, weight loss, a painful left foot drop, and then right wrist drop. Nerve conduction studies show asymmetric low-amplitude motor and sensory responses. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is elevated. What is the standard initial treatment if nerve and muscle biopsy confirms necrotizing vasculitis?
options: Intravenous immunoglobulin alone given every four weeks for six months
High-dose glucocorticoids combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab
items.explanation: Vasculitic neuropathy presenting as mononeuritis multiplex needs prompt immunosuppression. For systemic vasculitis, glucocorticoids combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab induce remission, while nonsystemic cases may respond to steroids with a second agent. Immunoglobulin or plasma exchange alone is not adequate for necrotizing vasculitis, and symptomatic therapy leaves the inflammation untreated. Maintenance therapy is then tapered while the clinical response and inflammatory markers are followed over many months.

items.stem: A 38-year-old immigrant has patches of hypopigmented, anesthetic skin on the arm and a palpable thickened ulnar nerve at the elbow, with asymmetric sensory and motor deficits. Which pathogen is responsible?
items.explanation: Leprosy is the most common treatable cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide, producing anesthetic skin lesions and thickened nerves, with a cool-temperature predilection that spares warm regions. Diphtheria causes a bulbar and demyelinating neuropathy after pharyngitis. Lyme disease and syphilis cause other neurologic syndromes without thickened nerves. Treatment with multidrug therapy halts progression, although established nerve damage usually remains and requires rehabilitation.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, burning feet, early satiety, postural lightheadedness, and heavy proteinuria. Serum free light chains show an elevated lambda level. Which diagnosis best explains the neuropathy?
items.explanation: A painful small fiber predominant neuropathy with autonomic failure, carpal tunnel syndrome, nephrotic range proteinuria, and a clonal light chain points to AL amyloidosis, confirmed by tissue biopsy and typing. Hereditary transthyretin disease lacks a monoclonal protein and rarely causes proteinuria early. Diabetes does not fit the proteinuria pattern, and POEMS is a demyelinating process with sclerotic bone lesions.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has numbness of the right face and an absent right corneal reflex. Blink reflex testing is performed by stimulating the supraorbital nerve on each side. Which result would localize the lesion to the afferent limb of the reflex on the right?
options: Absent response only in the right eye after stimulation on either side
Absent response in both eyes after right supraorbital stimulation
Normal response in both eyes with delayed latency
Absent response only in the left eye after left stimulation
items.explanation: The afferent limb of the blink reflex is the trigeminal nerve and the efferent limb the facial nerve. Right supraorbital stimulation normally evokes responses in both orbicularis oculi, so a lost response bilaterally after right stimulation, with a preserved response from the left, localizes to the right trigeminal afferent. A facial lesion removes the ipsilateral response from either side.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a subacute demyelinating polyneuropathy with tremor and sensory ataxia. She responds poorly to intravenous immunoglobulin. Serum testing shows IgG4 antibodies against neurofascin-155. Which therapy is most likely to benefit her?
options: Repeated immunoglobulin courses at higher dose
Oral prednisone alone for one month
items.explanation: Autoimmune nodopathy with IgG4 antibodies to paranodal proteins such as neurofascin-155 has a distinct picture of tremor, ataxia, and a poor response to immunoglobulin. These antibodies are best targeted with B cell depletion, and rituximab often produces good responses. Higher-dose immunoglobulin and short steroid courses tend to fail, and pyridostigmine acts at the junction. Titers of the antibody can be followed to judge the response to therapy.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man had paralytic poliomyelitis in childhood and recovered. For the past two years he has had increasing fatigue, new weakness in previously affected limbs, and muscle pain. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Post-polio syndrome appears decades after the acute illness, with fatigue, pain, and new weakness in muscles that were previously affected, attributed to overuse and degeneration of enlarged motor units. Poliovirus does not recur. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis shows upper motor neuron signs and spreads to new regions, and demyelinating neuropathy shows slowing on conduction studies. Management is supportive, with energy conservation, pacing, orthoses, and gentle exercise, as vigorous training can worsen weakness.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has sudden, uncontrollable laughing and crying episodes out of proportion to her mood. Which therapy is approved for this problem?
items.explanation: Pseudobulbar affect is a disinhibition of emotional expression that occurs in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and the combination of dextromethorphan and quinidine is approved to treat it. Riluzole slows progression but does not treat emotional lability. Baclofen addresses spasticity, and glycopyrrolate reduces sialorrhea but not emotional expression. Treatment is reasonable when episodes disturb daily life, and the dose is adjusted for tolerability.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has drowsiness, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and hyperreflexia after a viral illness. MRI shows hyperintensity in the brainstem. She is positive for anti-GQ1b antibodies. Which entity does this describe?
items.explanation: Bickerstaff encephalitis lies on the same anti-GQ1b spectrum as Miller Fisher syndrome but adds central involvement with altered consciousness or hyperreflexia, and MRI may show brainstem changes. Miller Fisher syndrome has ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and areflexia with a clear mind. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is multifocal, and Wernicke encephalopathy follows thiamine deficiency. Immunotherapy is similar to that used for Guillain-Barre syndrome, and most patients recover well over weeks to months.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with progressive distal weakness has median motor studies showing prolonged distal latency, velocity of 28 m/s, and a proximal compound muscle action potential that is more spread out and lower in amplitude than the distal one. Which term describes the spread-out proximal waveform?
items.explanation: Unequal slowing among motor fibers makes the volleys arrive at the muscle at different times, so the proximal waveform is prolonged and lower in area. This is temporal dispersion and supports an acquired demyelinating process such as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. Crossover innervation is a median to ulnar anatomic variant, and giant units are a needle finding of chronic reinnervation.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has three days of refusal to walk, back pain, and absent knee and ankle reflexes after a respiratory infection. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a protein of 90 mg/dL and 2 cells per microliter. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Children with Guillain-Barre syndrome often present with pain, refusal to walk, and areflexia after an infection, and cerebrospinal fluid typically shows raised protein with a normal cell count. Transverse myelitis causes a sensory level and hyperreflexia. Spinal muscular atrophy and Duchenne dystrophy are chronic and do not produce acute areflexia. Immunotherapy should start promptly, because outcomes depend on early treatment and the rate of decline over days.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has numbness of the little finger and ring finger and clumsy grip. Ulnar motor studies show a conduction velocity across the elbow of 38 m/s, versus 62 m/s in the forearm segment. The dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory response is absent. What does this finding localize?
options: Ulnar nerve entrapment at or above the elbow, not at the wrist
Ulnar nerve compression within Guyon canal at the level of the wrist
items.explanation: Focal slowing of more than 10 m/s across the elbow compared with the forearm confirms ulnar neuropathy at the elbow. An abnormal dorsal ulnar cutaneous response, which branches about 6 to 8 cm above the wrist, shows the lesion lies proximal to Guyon canal. Lower trunk and root lesions would spare the local slowing and involve the median distribution.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man develops inability to extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints after a forearm injury. When he extends the wrist, it deviates radially. There is no sensory loss. Which nerve is involved?
options: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
items.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve is the motor continuation of the radial nerve below the elbow and has no cutaneous territory. It spares the extensor carpi radialis longus, so wrist extension persists with radial deviation, but finger extension fails. A spiral groove lesion causes a true wrist drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with Guillain-Barre syndrome has a forced vital capacity of 18 mL/kg and a single breath count of 12. She can still walk with assistance. What is the best next step?
options: Continue floor monitoring with hourly nursing checks and repeat spirometry the next morning after rest
Begin noninvasive treatment with a methylxanthine
Transfer to an intensive care unit for close respiratory monitoring or ventilation
items.explanation: A forced vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, a single breath count under 20, or rapid decline signals impending respiratory failure, and intubation is considered when it falls toward 15 mL/kg or when there is bulbar weakness. Patients should be monitored in an intensive setting regardless of walking ability. A methylxanthine does not treat neuromuscular respiratory weakness.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has orthopnea and morning headaches. His forced vital capacity has fallen to 45 percent of predicted. What intervention has been shown to prolong survival and improve quality of life?
options: Supplemental oxygen alone at night through nasal prongs
items.explanation: Noninvasive ventilation is standard once there is orthopnea, symptomatic hypoventilation, or a forced vital capacity below about 50 percent, and it prolongs survival and eases symptoms. Oxygen alone can worsen carbon dioxide retention in hypoventilation. Suppressing cough is harmful, and diaphragm pacing has been shown to shorten survival in trials. Respiratory function should be rechecked every few months, and tolerance of the mask improves with time.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has chronic aching of the medial forearm, thin atrophic muscles of the thenar eminence, and numbness along the medial forearm. Electrodiagnostic testing shows a very low median motor amplitude, a low ulnar sensory response, and an absent medial antebrachial cutaneous response. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with cord compression
items.explanation: Compression of the lower trunk by a cervical rib or fibrous band causes wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis, with milder involvement of hypothenar muscles and medial forearm numbness. Median motor and ulnar sensory responses are low, and the medial antebrachial cutaneous response is lost. Carpal tunnel syndrome spares the ulnar sensory and medial forearm responses.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has progressive Guillain-Barre syndrome and has received a standard course of intravenous immunoglobulin. Seven days later she has not improved and her condition has plateaued. Which management step is supported?
options: A repeat full course of immunoglobulin given at two grams per kilogram over five days
Supportive care, because a second immunoglobulin course has not been shown to help
Sequential plasma exchange immediately after immunoglobulin
items.explanation: Randomized evidence does not show benefit from giving a second immunoglobulin course to patients who plateau or do not improve after the first course, and a trial of a second dose raised concern for harm. Sequential immunoglobulin and plasma exchange is no better than either alone. Oral corticosteroids are not helpful in Guillain-Barre syndrome. Further treatment decisions should rest on supportive measures, careful respiratory monitoring, and rehabilitation planning.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with definite amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, symptom onset 14 months ago, asks about disease-modifying therapy. Which statement about edaravone is most accurate?
options: It is an oral glutamate release inhibitor that prolongs survival by months
It is an antisense oligonucleotide targeting SOD1 messenger RNA
It is a monoclonal antibody that cures the disease in early stages
It is an intravenous free radical scavenger that slowed functional decline in a selected early population
items.explanation: Edaravone is given intravenously in cycles and acts as an antioxidant, with benefit shown in a carefully selected group with early disease and preserved function. Riluzole is the oral agent that reduces glutamate release and modestly prolongs survival. Tofersen is the SOD1 antisense therapy. No monoclonal antibody cures amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Confirmation of eligibility, including the functional score and respiratory function, guides who receives the infusions.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy awakens with right facial droop involving the forehead, with loss of taste on the anterior tongue and hyperacusis. There is no rash. What is the best approach to treatment?
options: Observation without treatment because pregnancy contraindicates steroids
Prednisone started within 72 hours and eye lubrication and taping
Surgical decompression of the facial nerve
items.explanation: Bell palsy is more common in pregnancy, and an early course of oral glucocorticoids, started within 72 hours of onset, improves the chance of full recovery. Protecting the cornea is essential when eye closure fails. Surgery is not indicated, and antiviral therapy adds little to steroids alone in idiopathic cases. Antiviral drugs add little in addition to steroids for Bell palsy, and recovery usually begins within weeks.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man has progressive weakness and wasting of the proximal arms and legs with fasciculations and areflexia, but no upper motor neuron signs after three years. Electromyography shows widespread denervation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Progressive muscular atrophy, a lower motor neuron predominant motor neuron disease
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with bulbar onset
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
items.explanation: Isolated lower motor neuron degeneration without clinical upper motor neuron signs is progressive muscular atrophy, though many patients later develop upper motor neuron features. Bulbar-onset disease would show speech and swallowing problems early. Multifocal motor neuropathy is distinguished by conduction block, and inclusion body myositis shows myopathic features and a biopsy with inclusions. Many patients show upper motor neuron signs later, so serial examinations over the following months are important.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man on warfarin with a supratherapeutic international normalized ratio develops severe groin pain, then weakness of knee extension and numbness over the anteromedial thigh and medial leg. The knee jerk is absent and hip adduction is normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: Obturator neuropathy from pelvic surgery with adductor weakness and medial thigh numbness
Femoral neuropathy from retroperitoneal or iliopsoas hematoma
items.explanation: Bleeding into the iliacus or psoas compartment compresses the femoral nerve, causing quadriceps weakness, a lost patellar reflex, and sensory loss over the anteromedial thigh and saphenous territory. Normal hip adduction spares the obturator nerve. An L5 lesion would not remove the knee jerk, and sciatic lesions affect the hamstrings and below-knee muscles. Reversal of anticoagulation and imaging of the retroperitoneum are urgent when a hematoma is suspected.

items.stem: A 53-year-old man develops progressive weakness and memory and personality change, and his brother has frontotemporal dementia with motor neuron disease. Genetic testing is most likely to show an abnormality in which gene?
options: SMN1 homozygous exon 7 deletion on chromosome 5
items.explanation: A repeat expansion in C9orf72 is the most common genetic cause of both familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia, and families often show both phenotypes. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy, and the androgen receptor expansion causes Kennedy disease. SOD1 mutations cause a familial form without prominent dementia. Testing guides counseling for relatives, and many families are affected by both cognitive and motor symptoms.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has six weeks of progressive weakness of the left hand and wrist extension without sensory loss. Motor conduction of the left median nerve shows a normal compound muscle action potential with distal stimulation but a 60 percent drop in amplitude with stimulation at the elbow. Which finding does this best represent?
options: Uniform slowing of conduction in all fibers
Presynaptic neuromuscular junction failure of transmission
Partial conduction block in a motor nerve segment
items.explanation: A large amplitude drop between distal and proximal stimulation, with a preserved distal response, indicates conduction block from focal demyelination between the two sites. Wallerian degeneration lowers the distal response as well after several days. Uniform slowing alters velocity and latency but not amplitude. Junction failure causes decrement on repetitive stimulation, not a proximal to distal amplitude gap.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, weakness of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, and loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue, all on the right, after a skull base fracture. Which localization is most appropriate?
options: Cavernous sinus involving cranial nerves III, IV, and VI
Cerebellopontine angle involving cranial nerves VII and VIII
Jugular foramen involving cranial nerves IX, X, and XI
Hypoglossal canal involving cranial nerve XII
items.explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves exit together through the jugular foramen, so a lesion there causes palatal and vocal cord weakness, loss of posterior tongue taste, and trapezius and sternocleidomastoid weakness. Cavernous sinus lesions cause ocular motor palsies. Cerebellopontine angle lesions affect hearing and facial function, and the hypoglossal canal contains only the twelfth nerve.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has neck pain radiating down the back of the arm into the middle finger, with weakness of elbow extension and a reduced triceps reflex. Which root is most likely involved?
items.explanation: The triceps is supplied mainly by C7 through the radial nerve, and the triceps jerk and middle finger sensation also map to C7, the most commonly compressed cervical root. C5 affects deltoid and biceps, C6 affects the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes and the thumb, and C8 affects finger flexors, hand intrinsics, and the ring and little fingers.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has slowly progressive distal sensory ataxia and tremor. Nerve conduction shows markedly prolonged distal latencies, and serum shows an IgM kappa paraprotein. Which antibody is most likely present?
items.explanation: Distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy with an IgM paraprotein is typically associated with antibodies to myelin-associated glycoprotein, producing a sensory ataxic neuropathy with disproportionately prolonged distal latencies. Treatment with rituximab can slow progression. Anti-GQ1b is linked to Miller Fisher syndrome, anti-Hu to paraneoplastic neuronopathy, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies to myasthenia. Prognosis is slow, and treatment aims at stabilization rather than quick improvement of balance.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, facial numbness, and unsteadiness. Examination shows an absent corneal reflex on the same side. Which lesion most likely accounts for her syndrome?
options: A vestibular schwannoma in the cerebellopontine angle
A lesion of the lateral medullary region
A lesion of the cervical spinal cord
items.explanation: An enlarging vestibular schwannoma causes progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, and with growth compresses the trigeminal nerve, producing facial numbness and a reduced corneal reflex, and then the cerebellum causes gait unsteadiness. A pituitary tumor causes visual field loss. Lateral medullary and cervical cord lesions do not produce progressive hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging with contrast through the internal auditory canal confirms the lesion and guides surgery or radiosurgery.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has right ear pain, persistent discharge from otitis media, double vision on lateral gaze to the right, and retro-orbital pain. Which diagnosis is suggested?
options: Petrous apicitis (Gradenigo syndrome) with abducens and trigeminal involvement
Cavernous sinus thrombosis from a facial infection
items.explanation: The triad of otitis media, abducens palsy, and retro-orbital facial pain defines Gradenigo syndrome, caused by infection spreading to the petrous apex, where the sixth nerve passes beneath the petroclinoid ligament near the trigeminal ganglion. Cavernous sinus thrombosis usually follows facial infection and affects multiple ocular motor nerves. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes headache and papilledema.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman treated with radiation for breast cancer 12 years ago has gradual painless weakness and numbness of the entire arm. Electromyography shows myokymic discharges in the weak muscles. Which diagnosis is favored?
options: Neoplastic brachial plexopathy from tumor recurrence
items.explanation: Painless progressive upper trunk or panplexus weakness, delayed by years after irradiation, with myokymic discharges on needle examination, favors radiation plexopathy. Tumor invasion typically causes early severe pain, a lower trunk pattern, and Horner syndrome. Neuralgic amyotrophy begins abruptly with severe pain, and a disc lesion would show paraspinal denervation and radicular distribution. Imaging of the plexus and timing relative to treatment help separate it from tumor recurrence.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man who smokes has severe shoulder pain radiating down the medial arm into the ring and little fingers, with wasting of intrinsic hand muscles and a right ptosis with miosis. What is the most likely cause?
options: A cervical rib compressing the lower trunk of the brachial plexus without any lung involvement
A superior sulcus tumor invading the lower trunk and sympathetic chain
items.explanation: A Pancoast tumor at the lung apex invades the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the stellate ganglion, causing pain along the ulnar border, hand weakness, and Horner syndrome. A cervical rib would not usually cause a Horner syndrome or severe constant pain. A C5-C6 disc affects the C6 root, and neuralgic amyotrophy involves the upper trunk.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman has progressive loss of vibration and position sense, ataxia, and burning in the hands over several months. Sensory responses are absent. Chest imaging shows a lung mass, and serum is positive for anti-Hu antibodies. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy associated with small cell lung cancer
items.explanation: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) antibodies cause an immune attack on dorsal root ganglion neurons, producing a subacute sensory neuronopathy with ataxia and absent sensory responses, and they are classically associated with small cell lung cancer. Diabetic neuropathy is length dependent and slower. Acute motor axonal neuropathy spares sensory fibers, and copper deficiency affects the dorsal columns and anemia.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man who had gastric bypass surgery years ago presents with spastic gait, loss of vibration and position sense, and anemia with neutropenia. Vitamin B12 is normal. A prior dietary history reveals heavy use of zinc-containing denture cream. Which deficiency is most likely?
options: Vitamin E deficiency with ataxia and retinopathy
items.explanation: Copper deficiency causes a myeloneuropathy that mimics subacute combined degeneration, with a dorsal column syndrome, spasticity, and cytopenias. Risk factors include bariatric surgery, malabsorption, and excess zinc, which induces intestinal metallothionein and blocks copper uptake. Vitamin E deficiency produces a spinocerebellar syndrome, and folate lack rarely causes isolated neuropathy. Replacing copper and removing the source of excess zinc halts progression, though established myelopathy often recovers poorly.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a week of numbness in the left chin and lower lip. Examination shows a normal facial nerve and no masticatory weakness. Which diagnosis best explains this finding, and what must be excluded?
options: Trigeminal neuralgia, with exclusion of vascular compression
Bell palsy, with exclusion of Lyme disease
Mental neuropathy (numb chin syndrome), with exclusion of malignancy such as breast or lymphoma
Tolosa-Hunt syndrome, with exclusion of aneurysm
items.explanation: Numbness of the chin and lip from involvement of the mental branch of the inferior alveolar nerve is called numb chin syndrome and can signal metastatic disease or lymphoma, as well as dental or connective tissue causes, so imaging and a malignancy search are warranted. Trigeminal neuralgia causes pain, Bell palsy causes weakness, and Tolosa-Hunt involves orbital pain.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman has ataxia, loss of position sense in all four limbs, and areflexia, but normal strength. Motor studies are normal, and sensory nerve action potentials are absent in the arms and legs in a non length dependent pattern. Which localization best fits?
options: Anterior horn cells, a pure motor neuronopathy
Dorsal root ganglia, a sensory neuronopathy
Distal axons, a length dependent polyneuropathy
items.explanation: Diffuse sensory loss with ataxia, absent sensory responses, and normal motor studies points to loss of the sensory neuron cell bodies in the ganglia. The pattern is patchy and not length dependent and affects the face and trunk as well. A distal polyneuropathy would affect the feet first, and junction or anterior horn disease would spare sensory responses.

items.stem: A 34-year-old nurse has a year of widespread twitching in the calves and arms with muscle cramps. Strength, reflexes, and tone are normal, and electromyography shows fasciculation potentials with no denervation or reinnervation. What is the most appropriate counseling?
options: The findings support benign fasciculation syndrome, with reassurance and follow-up
She has early amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and should start riluzole
She needs an urgent muscle biopsy to exclude dystrophy
She should begin immunoglobulin for suspected neuropathy
items.explanation: Isolated fasciculations with a normal examination and no fibrillations, positive sharp waves, or chronic neurogenic changes on needle examination are almost always benign. Fasciculation potentials alone do not establish a motor neuron disease. Follow-up is appropriate because new weakness or atrophy would change the picture. Biopsy and immunotherapy have no role. Cramps often accompany this condition, and anxiety tends to amplify awareness of twitching without any underlying disease.

items.stem: Which nerve conduction pattern best separates a primary axonal neuropathy from a primary demyelinating neuropathy in a patient with distal weakness?
options: Markedly slowed velocity with prolonged distal latency and dispersion
Normal amplitude with proximal conduction block and delayed F waves in each nerve tested
Low compound muscle action potentials with only mildly slowed velocity
Slowing below 70 percent of the lower limit of normal in every nerve
items.explanation: Axon loss reduces the number of conducting fibers, so amplitudes fall while velocity is only mildly reduced because the fastest surviving fibers still conduct normally. Marked slowing, prolonged distal latencies, dispersion, block, and delayed F waves mark demyelination. Velocity rarely falls below about 75 percent of normal from axon loss alone. Demyelinating disease should be suspected only when slowing exceeds what axon loss alone can explain.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has low back pain radiating down the posterior leg, a diminished left ankle jerk, and weakness of plantar flexion. Which electrodiagnostic test best documents loss of the afferent and efferent reflex arc for this root?
options: Blink reflex recorded from the orbicularis oculi
Facial motor latency recorded from the nasalis
Sural sensory response recorded at the ankle
H reflex recorded from the soleus muscle
items.explanation: The H reflex is the electrical analogue of the ankle jerk, recorded in the soleus after tibial nerve stimulation, and it tests the S1 root arc. It is delayed or absent in S1 radiculopathy. The blink reflex tests trigeminal and facial pathways. Facial latency and the sural response do not examine the S1 root, and the sensory response is preserved in root lesions.

items.stem: A 45-year-old typist has nocturnal hand numbness. Routine median and ulnar studies are borderline. Which comparative test is most sensitive for mild median neuropathy at the wrist?
options: Median motor conduction velocity across the elbow segment
Median versus ulnar sensory latency to the ring finger
Ulnar sensory amplitude to the fifth digit
Radial motor latency to the extensor indicis
items.explanation: Comparing median and ulnar sensory latencies to the ring finger over the same distance cancels out limb temperature and age effects and detects slowing localized to the carpal tunnel before routine studies turn abnormal. Elbow segment studies and ulnar or radial responses assess other nerves and do not reveal median compression at the wrist. The comparison remains valid even in patients whose limbs are cool or who are elderly.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman with long-standing Sjogren syndrome has a slowly progressive non length dependent loss of sensation, with ataxia of the hands and face, and no weakness. Which pathology best explains this?
options: Inflammatory ganglionopathy of the dorsal root ganglia
Axonal degeneration of motor neurons in the spinal cord
Segmental demyelination of large nerve roots
Presynaptic calcium channel blockade at the junction
items.explanation: Sjogren syndrome is a recognized cause of sensory neuronopathy, where lymphocytic infiltration injures the dorsal root ganglion neurons, giving patchy sensory loss with proprioceptive ataxia and facial or trigeminal involvement. Motor neuron degeneration would cause weakness, demyelination would show slowing, and presynaptic blockade describes Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Immunosuppressive therapy is often tried, although evidence is limited and outcomes vary from stabilization to modest improvement.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man has a progressive course of limb weakness and areflexia over 6 months, with demyelinating features on nerve conduction. He is treated with prednisone and improves. Which feature most strongly separates chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy from Guillain-Barre syndrome?
options: Progression for longer than eight weeks
items.explanation: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is defined by progression or relapse over more than 8 weeks, whereas Guillain-Barre syndrome reaches its nadir within 4 weeks. High cerebrospinal fluid protein with normal cell count, symmetric proximal and distal weakness, and areflexia occur in both conditions and cannot separate them by themselves. Nerve conduction patterns and spinal fluid protein cannot reliably make the distinction by themselves.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has progressive painless weakness of the right arm and bulbar speech, with fasciculations in the tongue and thighs, hyperreflexia in the legs, and no sensory loss. Which finding best satisfies criteria for a diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?
options: Fasciculations alone in a single limb
Weakness with conduction block on nerve studies
Upper and lower motor neuron signs in multiple body regions with progression
Elevated creatine kinase with myopathic units
items.explanation: Diagnosis rests on progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs spreading within or across bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions, with exclusion of mimics. Isolated fasciculations are common in benign conditions. Conduction block suggests multifocal motor neuropathy, and myopathic units with high creatine kinase suggest a muscle disease. Revised criteria also allow diagnosis in patients with isolated upper or lower signs when genetic testing is positive.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman had a car crash 10 days ago and now has a flail right arm with absent sensation in the whole limb. Sensory nerve action potentials in the arm are preserved, and motor responses are absent. What does this combination suggest?
options: Early conduction block in the median nerve
items.explanation: Preserved sensory responses in an anesthetic limb mean the sensory neuron and its peripheral axon are intact and the lesion lies proximal to the ganglion, typical of root avulsion. A postganglionic lesion would cause Wallerian degeneration and loss of sensory responses after about a week. An isolated distal ulnar lesion would not produce a global limb deficit.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has foot deformities and weakness. His mother has mild symptoms, and examination of the family shows no male to male transmission. Median motor conduction velocities are 35 m/s in the man and intermediate in his mother. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 arises from GJB1 mutations, with intermediate conduction velocities, more severe disease in men, and milder disease in carrier women, and absent male to male transmission. PMP22 duplication causes autosomal dominant type 1A with uniform slowing. MFN2 causes axonal type 2A, and MPZ mutations are autosomal dominant with variable severity. Genetic confirmation allows family counseling, since women carriers may have mild or absent symptoms.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man develops rapidly progressive symmetric limb weakness with areflexia three weeks after a diarrheal illness. Nerve conduction studies show low motor amplitudes with no demyelinating features, and anti-GM1 antibodies are present. Which variant is most likely?
items.explanation: Antecedent Campylobacter jejuni infection with pure motor weakness, low motor amplitudes without demyelination, and anti-GM1 or anti-GD1a antibodies defines acute motor axonal neuropathy, which is common in Asia and may recover quickly or slowly. Demyelinating Guillain-Barre syndrome shows slowing and block. The pharyngeal variant is bulbar and arm predominant, and sensory ataxic forms involve proprioception.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has 8 years of slowly progressive spastic gait and dysarthria with brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses, and no fasciculations or atrophy. Electromyography is normal. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with a family history
items.explanation: Isolated progressive upper motor neuron signs for more than 3 years, without lower motor neuron involvement on examination or electromyography, define primary lateral sclerosis, which progresses much more slowly than amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Progressive muscular atrophy shows pure lower motor neuron findings. Kennedy disease is an X-linked lower motor neuron disorder, and hereditary spastic paraplegia requires a family pattern or mutation.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has early weakness and tingling in both feet, with absent ankle reflexes. Routine motor and sensory conduction studies of the legs are normal. Which late response is most likely to show the earliest abnormality in a proximal demyelinating lesion such as a nerve root?
options: Increased jitter on single fiber testing
items.explanation: F waves travel up the motor axon to the anterior horn cell and back, so they sample proximal segments that routine distal studies skip. Early Guillain-Barre syndrome, radiculopathy, or root involvement may change only F waves or the H reflex. The sural response reflects distal sensory axons, while jitter and decrement belong to junction disorders.
